sources.title: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Books I-II (F. H. Peters translation)
sources.notes: Primary classical source. Public-domain F. H. Peters translation from Project Gutenberg #8438. Books I-II establish eudaimonia, the human function, virtue as a settled disposition, habituation, and the doctrine of the mean.

sources.title: Calum McCracken, 'Virtue Ethics' (2024)
sources.notes: Contemporary openly licensed exposition from TRU Open Press. CC BY 4.0 attribution is retained in the committed file.

sources.title: G. E. M. Anscombe, 'Modern Moral Philosophy' (1958)
sources.notes: Published in Philosophy 33(124), 1-19. Copyrighted journal article; metadata only. Anscombe criticizes modern moral philosophy's law-like obligation vocabulary when detached from a divine legislator, and calls for a return to a richer philosophy of psychology and virtue.

sources.title: Philippa Foot, Natural Goodness (2001)
sources.notes: Oxford University Press book; copyrighted, metadata only. Foot develops a neo-Aristotelian naturalism in which evaluations of human action and character are tied to the life-form and natural goodness of human beings.

sources.title: Rosalind Hursthouse, On Virtue Ethics (1999)
sources.notes: Oxford University Press book; copyrighted, metadata only. Hursthouse gives a systematic account of virtue ethics, practical wisdom, eudaimonia, and the action-guiding form 'an action is right iff it is what a virtuous agent would characteristically do.'

sources.title: Alasdair MacIntyre, After Virtue (1981; 3rd edition 2007)
sources.notes: University of Notre Dame Press book; copyrighted, metadata only. MacIntyre reconstructs virtue as intelligible within practices, traditions, and a narrative conception of a whole human life, criticizing the fragmentation of modern moral discourse.
